A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FairMT-Bench and provide readable main text, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C. Existing experiments and relocated appendix material can be matched reliably. Inconsistent dataset totals affect interpretation, but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of six LLMs on FairMT-10K and fifteen on FairMT-1K, alongside dialogue-turn analyses, case studies, and human validation.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds conversational-capability, over-refusal, human-validation, and DPO alignment results.

M1.justification: The six-task benchmark and judging framework remain intact. However, Figure 10 changes the documented third-turn Scattered Questions template from referring to [Target Group] to [Biased Attribution]. This is a limited prompt-template revision; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun using it.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluation on MT-Bench-101, covering conversational perceptivity, adaptability, and interactivity (Appendices B.1 and B.6). The FairMT datasets retain their three source datasets, six fairness tasks, bias types, and attribute categories.

E2.justification: The six-model FairMT-10K and fifteen-model FairMT-1K comparison sets are unchanged. Appendix B.6 adds a supplementary comparison between base Llama-2-7b-chat and single-turn and multi-turn DPO-aligned variants. Benchmarks listed in the new related-work table are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 introduces capability scoring, refusal evaluation on benign Fixed Format turns, and single-turn versus multi-turn DPO training/evaluation. Human validation gains task-level accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. Table 1 revises dataset composition and the total from 10,280 to 10,195, although Table 4 totals 10,157; these reported revisions do not establish benchmark reruns.

E4.justification: New analyses examine over-refusal and relationships between conversational capabilities and fairness (B.1/Table 6), and fairness–utility trade-offs after DPO alignment (B.6/Table 9). Appendix B.4 adds an implicit gender-bias case study. These substantially extend the retained turn-count, attribute, and dialogue-case analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Three-annotator assessment and majority voting are retained, with voting described in v2's ethics statement. The added classification metrics concern evaluation performance rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 3 and the relocated Llama-Guard and single-turn tables retain their values. V2 replaces v1's 87.5% human–GPT-4 agreement summary with task-level metrics, including total accuracy 0.9569; unspecified sampling prevents interpreting this as a comparable improvement. New Tables 6 and 9 report capability, refusal, and alignment outcomes, including average bias of 76.36%, 11.21%, and 12.12% for base, single-turn-aligned, and multi-turn-aligned models. Figure 4 replaces the duplicated toxicity curves with distinct results.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The taxonomy and bias-rate concept are retained; the added alignment study introduces no new formal mathematical treatment.

C1.justification: V2 removes the explicit claim to be the first multi-turn fairness benchmark from the introduction and conclusion. The central contributions—six-task taxonomy, FairMT-10K/1K, and evidence of multi-turn fairness weaknesses—retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: Appendix B.6 newly interprets alignment improvements as potentially reflecting dataset fitting and increased refusal, while documenting reduced conversational capability and an unresolved fairness–utility trade-off. B.1 discusses susceptibility associated with adaptability/interactivity, and B.4 explains failures on subtle gender stereotypes. These materially qualify how fairness scores should be interpreted.

D1.justification: V2 adds a repository link and states that code and data are public. Appendix A.5 specifies GPT-4 Turbo, H100 hardware, batch size 1, FP32 precision, generation time, and evaluation costs. B.5 details challenge-set ranking and selection, and B.6 explains preference-pair construction. Conversely, v1's explicit 10% human-validation sampling statement is removed.

R1.justification: Appendix C adds a structured benchmark-coverage comparison in Table 10 and discussion of multi-turn safety evaluations such as S-Eval and CoSafe. References also expand for the new analyses and comparison table. The central positioning against predominantly single-turn fairness evaluation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Substantial passages in the abstract, introduction, task explanations, evaluation description, related work, and ethics statement are rewritten. Human-evaluation results move from A.5 to A.4.2, with new cost and experimental subsections. Terminology, affiliations, and conference headers are also revised.

P2.justification: V2 adds five tables and an implicit-bias case figure, revises Figure 1 and several illustrated prompt templates, and redraws Figure 4's toxicity panel. Existing result tables and case figures are relocated or renumbered, while their retained content remains distinguishable from the additions.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful checks on whether fairness reflects over-refusal or reduced conversational utility, more informative task-level judge validation, and practical reproducibility details. Correcting Figure 4 also improves accuracy. These gains are limited by conflicting dataset totals—10,195 in Table 1 versus 10,157 in Tables 4 and 10—the missing validation sampling description, and unclear training/evaluation separation for the alignment study.
